text: Louis Daniel Armstrong (August 4, 1901 – July 6, 1971), nicknamed "Satchmo", "Satch", and "Pops", was an American jazz and blues trumpeter and vocalist, considered one of the most influential figures in jazz. His career spanned five decades and several eras in jazz history. He received numerous accolades, including the Grammy Award for Best Male Vocal Performance for "Hello, Dolly!" in 1965, and a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972. His influence extended across musical genres, with inductions into the DownBeat Jazz Hall of Fame, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame. Born in New Orleans, Armstrong rose to prominence in the 1920s as an inventive trumpet and cornet player, shifting jazz from collective improvisation to solo performance. In 1922, he moved to Chicago with mentor Joe "King" Oliver to join Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, where he gained fame through cutting contests and attracted the attention of Fletcher Henderson. He later moved to New York City, becoming a featured soloist and recording artist, and by the 1950s was an international musical icon, regularly appearing on radio, television, and film. Known for his rich, gravelly voice and skillful improvisation, Armstrong was also a pioneer in scat singing, first recording it on the Hot Five track "Heebie Jeebies" in 1926. His best-known songs include "What a Wonderful World", "La Vie en Rose", "Hello, Dolly!", "On the Sunny Side of the Street", "Dream a Little Dream of Me", "When You're Smiling", and "When the Saints Go Marching In". He collaborated with Ella Fitzgerald on three records: Ella and Louis (1956), Ella and Louis Again (1957), and Porgy and Bess (1959), and appeared in films such as A Rhapsody in Black and Blue (1932), Cabin in the Sky (1943), High Society (1956), Paris Blues (1961), A Man Called Adam (1966), and Hello, Dolly! (1969). Armstrong was one of the first popular African-American entertainers to cross over to wide popularity with white and international audiences. Though he rarely discussed racial issues publicly, he took a well-publicized stand for desegregation during the Little Rock Crisis and could access upper echelons of American society at a time when this was difficult for Black men. Armstrong was born on August 4, 1901, though he often claimed July 4, 1900, and his parents were Mary Estelle "Mayann" Albert and William Armstrong; Mary was from Boutte, Louisiana, and gave birth to her daughter Beatrice "Mama Lucy" Armstrong (1903–1987) when she was about 16. William abandoned the family shortly after. Armstrong was raised by his grandmother until age five, when he returned to his mother. He lived in poverty in The Battlefield neighborhood on Rampart Street and attended the Fisk School for Boys, a segregated school. At age six, he worked for the Karnoffskys, a Jewish family, collecting rags and bones and delivering coal. He sang "Russian Lullaby" with them when their son David was put to bed and credits them with teaching him to sing from the heart. The lyrics he quoted match Irving Berlin's 1927 song, about 20 years after he remembered singing it. In his 1969 memoir, Louis Armstrong + the Jewish Family in New Orleans, LA., the Year of 1907, he described being seven years old when he witnessed discrimination against the Karnoffskys and learned about real life and determination. He may have performed his first musical act at the side of the Karnoffskys' junk wagon, playing a tin horn to attract customers, and Morris Karnoffsky gave him an advance to buy a cornet. At age 11, he dropped out of school. His mother moved into a one-room house on Perdido Street with Armstrong, Lucy, and her common-law husband Tom Lee. Armstrong joined a quartet of boys who sang in the streets; Bunk Johnson taught him to play by ear at Dago Tony's honky tonk. He was arrested on December 31, 1912, for firing a blank from his stepfather's gun and was sent to the Colored Waif's Home, where life was spartan and corporal punishment was used. There, Peter Davis became his first teacher and chose him as bandleader. At age 13, he attracted the attention of Kid Ory. On June 14, 1914, he was released to his father and stepmother, Gertrude, and lived with two stepbrothers for several months before being rejected by his father and returning to his mother. He shared a bed with her and Lucy in a small home in The Battlefield and sought musical work. He found a job at a dance hall owned by Henry Ponce, met the drummer Black Benny, who became his guide and bodyguard, and at age 15 pimped for a prostitute named Nootsy, who stabbed him in the shoulder and was nearly choked to death by his mother. He briefly studied shipping management at a local community college but quit due to financial difficulties. While selling coal in Storyville, he heard spasm bands playing music from household objects and listened to early jazz from bands like Pete Lala's, where King Oliver performed. In the late 1910s, he played in brass bands and riverboats in New Orleans, touring with Fate Marable's band on the steamboat Sidney with the Streckfus Steamers. Marable praised Armstrong's musical knowledge and insisted he learn sight reading, which Armstrong described as "going to the university." In 1918, when King Oliver left Kid Ory's band, Armstrong replaced him and also became second trumpet in the Tuxedo Brass Band. By age 20, he could read music and began performing extended trumpet solos, injecting his own style and starting to sing. In 1922, he moved to Chicago at Oliver's invitation, though he returned to New Orleans periodically. Playing second cornet in Oliver's Creole Jazz Band at the black-only Lincoln Gardens in Chicago, he earned enough to quit day jobs. Chicago offered better job opportunities for Black people, including in factories and entertainment. Oliver's band was influential in the early 1920s. Armstrong lived luxuriously in Chicago with his first private bath and began writing letters to friends in New Orleans. He could blow 200 high Cs in a row and gained a reputation through cutting contests. His first studio recordings with Oliver for Gennett Records occurred on April 5–6, 1923, during a long train journey to Richmond, Indiana, with poor equipment, acoustics, and a cramped studio. The recordings were acoustic, with the band playing directly into a funnel connected to the needle. Because Armstrong played so loudly, Oliver could not be heard, so Armstrong stood 15 feet away. Lil Hardin, whom he married in 1924, urged him to seek more prominent billing and develop his own style. She encouraged him to play classical music in church concerts and dress more stylishly. Her influence strained his relationship with Oliver, especially over salary and withheld earnings. Armstrong's mother visited Chicago in 1923 after being told he was out of work, hungry, and sick; Hardin arranged and decorated an apartment for her. Armstrong and Oliver parted amicably in 1924. He was invited to join Fletcher Henderson's Orchestra, the top African-American band of the time, where he switched to trumpet to blend in. His influence on Coleman Hawkins, Henderson's tenor sax soloist, is evident in their recordings. Armstrong adapted to Henderson's tight style, playing trumpet and experimenting with trombone, and his emotional style affected the entire band. His performances included singing and stories about New Orleans preachers. The Henderson Orchestra played for white patrons only at venues like the Roseland Ballroom, with arrangements by Don Redman, and Duke Ellington's orchestra came to watch Armstrong. During this time, he recorded with Clarence Williams, the Williams Blue Five, Sidney Bechet, and blues singers Alberta Hunter, Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith. In 1925, he returned to Chicago at Lil's insistence, where she billed him as "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player." He joined her band and later formed Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five, recording hits such as "Potato Head Blues" and "Muggles" (a slang term for marijuana). The Hot Five included Kid Ory (trombone), Johnny Dodds (clarinet), Johnny St. Cyr (banjo), Lil Armstrong on piano, and no drummer. Over a 12-month period starting in November 1925, they produced 24 records. Armstrong's leadership style was easygoing, with St. Cyr noting the group felt relaxed and broad-minded. Recordings like "Cornet Chop Suey", "Struttin' With Some Barbecue", "Hotter Than That", and "Potato Head Blues" featured highly creative solos by Armstrong. According to Thomas Brothers, "Struttin' with Some Barbeque" was so well-planned with bluesyness and showiness that it was likely showcased at the Sunset Café. His recordings with pianist Earl "Fatha" Hines, including the 1928 "Weather Bird" duet and his trumpet introduction and solo in "West End Blues", remain among the most influential improvisations in jazz history. Young musicians across the country memorized his solos. Armstrong also played with Erskine Tate's Little Symphony at the Vendome Theatre, providing music for silent films and live shows, including jazz versions of classical pieces like "Madame Butterfly," giving him experience with longer musical forms and large audiences. He began scat singing and was among the first to record it on "Heebie Jeebies" in 1926. The recording's popularity made the Hot Five the most famous jazz band in the U.S., despite rarely performing live. After separating from Lil, Armstrong played at the Sunset Café for Joe Glaser, Al Capone's associate, in the Carroll Dickerson Orchestra, later renamed Louis Armstrong and his Stompers. Hines was the music director and Glaser managed the orchestra. Hines and Armstrong became close collaborators. At the Sunset Café, Armstrong accompanied singer Adelaide Hall, who developed her scat singing with his guidance. In the first half of 1927, Armstrong formed his Hot Seven group, adding drummer Al "Baby" Dodds and tuba player Pete Briggs while keeping most of the original Hot Five lineup, with John Thomas replacing Kid Ory on trombone. Later that year, he recorded nine more records with a new Hot Five lineup. In the second half of 1928, he recorded with Zutty Singleton (drums), Earl Hines (piano), Jimmy Strong (clarinet), Fred Robinson (trombone), and Mancy Carr (banjo). Armstrong made a significant impact during the 1920s Harlem Renaissance, influencing writer Langston Hughes, who admired him and acknowledged him as one of the era's most recognized musicians. Hughes wrote books celebrating jazz and recognized Armstrong as a leader of the Harlem Renaissance's embrace of African-American culture. The sound of jazz, including Armstrong's music, helped shape Hughes as a writer, with his work reflecting the jazz style. As "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player," Armstrong solidified his legacy and continued focusing on his vocal career, bringing together Black and white audiences. In 1929, he returned to New York to play in the pit orchestra for the musical Hot Chocolates, an all-black revue written by Andy Razaf and pianist Fats Waller.

Zutty Singleton played drums, Earl Hines played piano, Jimmy Strong played clarinet, Fred Robinson played trombone, and Mancy Carr played banjo. During the 1920s Harlem Renaissance, Louis Armstrong made a significant impact, influencing well-known writer Langston Hughes, who admired Armstrong and recognized him as one of the most prominent musicians of the era. Hughes wrote books that celebrated jazz and acknowledged Armstrong as a leader in the Harlem Renaissance's embrace of African-American culture, and the sound of jazz, including Armstrong's music, helped shape Hughes's writing style, which mirrored the rhythms and improvisation of jazz. Armstrong, known as "The World's Greatest Trumpet Player" during this time, transformed jazz and maintained a strong focus on his vocal career, drawing both Black and white audiences. In 1929, Armstrong returned to New York to play in the pit orchestra for the all-Black revue *Hot Chocolates*, written by Andy Razaf and Fats Waller, where he made a cameo as a vocalist and regularly stole the show with his rendition of "Ain't Misbehavin'"; his version became his biggest-selling record. He later worked at Connie's Inn in Harlem, a venue rivaling the Cotton Club, which was fronted by gangster Dutch Schultz, and achieved success with vocal recordings, including songs by Hoagy Carmichael. His 1930s recordings used the RCA ribbon microphone, introduced in 1931, which added warmth to vocals and became central to the "crooning" sound of artists like Bing Crosby. Armstrong's interpretation of "Stardust" became one of the most successful versions ever recorded, highlighting his unique vocal style. His radical reworking of "Lazy River," recorded in 1931, began with a trumpet solo, introduced a melody with sobbing horns, and featured Armstrong's growling interjections like "Yeah!... Uh-huh... Sure... Way down, way down," and in the first verse, he sang with a single note and strongly syncopated phrasing, while in the second stanza, he improvised a melody that evolved into a classic scat singing passage. His vocal innovations, rooted in his trumpet experience, influenced jazz vocal interpretation, with his gravelly voice becoming an archetype and his scat singing influencing white singers like Bing Crosby. The Great Depression severely affected the jazz scene; the Cotton Club closed in 1936, many musicians stopped playing, Bix Beiderbecke died, Fletcher Henderson's band disbanded, Sidney Bechet became a tailor and moved to Paris, and Kid Ory returned to New Orleans to raise chickens. In 1930, Armstrong moved to Los Angeles to seek new opportunities, playing at the New Cotton Club with Lionel Hampton on drums, drawing Hollywood crowds and radio audiences, and appearing in his first movie, *Ex-Flame*, while also being convicted of marijuana possession and receiving a suspended sentence. He returned to Chicago in late 1931, playing in bands similar to Guy Lombardo's and recording more standards; when the mob pressured him to leave, he visited New Orleans, received a hero's welcome, saw old friends, sponsored a baseball team called Armstrong's Secret Nine, and had a cigar named after him. After a national tour shadowed by the mob, he fled to Europe. Upon returning to the U.S., Armstrong undertook exhausting tours, but financial issues from his agent Johnny Collins's erratic behavior and his own spending, along with breach of contract violations, left him short of cash. He hired Joe Glaser as his manager, who helped resolve legal issues, mob problems, and debts. Armstrong also faced health issues with his fingers and lips, worsened by his playing style, leading him to develop his vocal style and make his first theatrical appearances, including in *Pennies from Heaven* (1936) and substituting for Rudy Vallee on CBS radio in 1937, becoming the first African American to host a sponsored national broadcast. After years on the road, Armstrong settled permanently in Queens, New York, in 1943 with his fourth wife, Lucille. Despite challenges from Tin Pan Alley, gangster influence, and anti-Black prejudice, he continued developing his music. Big band bookings declined in the 1940s due to shifting public tastes, with ballrooms closing and pop vocals gaining popularity, making it impossible to sustain a 16-piece touring band. A revival of interest in 1940s traditional jazz allowed Armstrong to return to small-group styles. He performed as a guest with Lionel Hampton's band at the second Cavalcade of Jazz in Los Angeles on October 12, 1946, and led a successful small-group concert at New York Town Hall on May 17, 1947, featuring Jack Teagarden, with the two performing a duet on "Rockin' Chair" that was recorded for Okeh Records. On August 13, 1947, Joe Glaser restructured Armstrong's big band into a six-piece traditional jazz group, the Louis Armstrong and His All-Stars, featuring initially Earl "Fatha" Hines, Barney Bigard, Edmond Hall, Jack Teagarden, Trummy Young, Arvell Shaw, Billy Kyle, Marty Napoleon, Big Sid "Buddy" Catlett, Cozy Cole, Tyree Glenn, Barrett Deems, Mort Herbert, Joe Darensbourg, Eddie Shu, Joe Muranyi, and percussionist Danny Barcelona. On February 28, 1948, Suzy Delair performed "C'est si bon" at the first Nice Jazz Festival, and Armstrong loved the song; on June 26, 1950, he recorded the American version with English lyrics by Jerry Seelen, which became a worldwide success and was performed by top international singers. Armstrong was the first jazz musician to appear on the cover of *Time* magazine on February 21, 1949. He and his All-Stars performed at the ninth Cavalcade of Jazz at Wrigley Field on June 7, 1953, alongside Shorty Rogers, Roy Brown, Don Tosti, Earl Bostic, and Nat "King" Cole. Over 30 years, Armstrong performed more than 300 times a year, made many recordings, and appeared in over 30 films. By the 1950s, Armstrong was a widely beloved American icon and cultural ambassador with a global fanbase, but a generation gap emerged with younger jazz musicians like Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, and Sonny Rollins, who viewed Armstrong's vaudevillian style as outdated and "Uncle Tomish," calling it a link to minstrelsy that they were ashamed of; Armstrong referred to bebop as "Chinese music," and when asked in 1954 if he could play bebop, he replied, "'Bebop?' he husked. 'I just play music. Guys who invent terms like that are walking the streets with their instruments under their arms.'" After finishing his contract with Decca Records, Armstrong went freelance and recorded for other labels. He maintained an intense international touring schedule but suffered a heart attack in 1959 in Italy and had to rest. In 1964, after over two years without studio work, Armstrong recorded "Hello, Dolly!" by Jerry Herman, originally sung by Carol Channing; his version stayed on the Hot 100 for 22 weeks, longer than any other record that year, reached No. 1, and made him the oldest person to achieve that feat at 62 years, nine months, and five days, displacing The Beatles from the top spot. Armstrong toured into his 60s, visiting parts of the Communist Bloc in 1965 and touring Africa, Europe, and Asia under U.S. State Department sponsorship, earning the nickname "Ambassador Satch" and inspiring Dave Brubeck to compose *The Real Ambassadors*, with performances in Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria. By 1968, Armstrong was approaching 70 and his health was failing due to heart and kidney ailments, forcing him to stop touring, though he continued recording, including "What a Wonderful World," which topped the British charts for a month. He did not perform publicly in 1969 and spent most of the year recovering; his longtime manager Joe Glaser died. By summer 1970, doctors deemed him fit to resume performances, and he began another world tour, though a heart attack forced a two-month break. Armstrong made his last recorded trumpet performances on his 1968 album *Disney Songs the Satchmo Way*. The Louis Armstrong House Museum notes that Louis pronounced his name as "Lewis"; on his 1964 record "Hello, Dolly!", he sings, "This is Lewis, Dolly," and in 1933, he recorded "Laughin' Louie." Many announcers, fans, and acquaintances called him "Louie," and Lucille Armstrong called him "Louie" in a 1983 videotaped interview; musicians and close friends usually called him "Pops." In a 1943–1944 memoir, Armstrong stated, "All white folks call me Louie," suggesting he did not use the nickname himself or that whites never addressed him by it. He was registered as "Lewie" on the 1920 U.S. census; "Lewie" is the French pronunciation of "Louis" and is common in Louisiana. In 1919, while performing at the Brick House in Gretna, Louisiana, Armstrong met Daisy Parker, a local prostitute, and began an affair. He visited her home several times and learned she had a common-law husband. On March 19, 1919, they married at City Hall. They adopted a three-year-old boy, Clarence, whose mother, Armstrong's cousin Flora, died shortly after giving birth; Clarence had a head injury and was mentally disabled, and Armstrong cared for him his entire life. Their marriage ended in 1923. On February 4, 1924, Armstrong married Lil Hardin Armstrong, King Oliver's pianist; she had divorced her first husband. She helped develop his career, but they separated in 1931 and divorced in 1938. Armstrong then married Alpha Smith, beginning the relationship during the 1920s at the Vendome and continuing afterward; their marriage lasted four years and ended in 1942. He married Lucille Wilson, a singer at the Cotton Club in New York, in October 1942, and remained married until his death in 1971. Armstrong had no biological children. In December 2012, Sharon Preston-Folta claimed to be his daughter from a 1950s affair with Lucille "Sweets" Preston, a Cotton Club dancer; in a 1955 letter to his manager Joe Glaser, Armstrong affirmed the baby was his daughter and ordered Glaser to pay $400 per month ($5,869 in 2024 dollars) to the mother and child. Armstrong was known for his colorful and charismatic personality, and his autobiography caused some biographers and historians concern due to his tendency to embellish stories, especially about his early childhood. He was a leading public figure, beloved by an American public that rarely engaged deeply with Black performers, and lived a private life of access and privilege rarely afforded to other Black Americans. Armstrong generally remained politically neutral, which sometimes alienated him from other Black Americans who expected him to be more vocal during the civil rights movement, though he criticized President Eisenhower for not acting forcefully on civil rights. The trumpet is hard on the lips, and Armstrong suffered lip damage due to his aggressive playing style and preference for narrow mouthpieces that dug into his inner lip. During his 1930s European tour, he suffered a severe ulceration that required him to stop playing for a year. He used salves and creams, cut scar tissue with a razor blade, and by the 1950s became an official spokesman for Ansatz-Creme Lip Salve. In a 1959 backstage meeting with Marshall Brown, Armstrong was advised to see a doctor for proper lip treatment, but he did not until his final years, when his health was failing and doctors considered surgery too risky. In 1959, Armstrong was hospitalized for pneumonia in Italy, with doctors concerned about his lungs and heart, but he recovered by the end of June. The nicknames "Satchmo" and "Satch" are short for "Satchelmouth"; the origin is uncertain. One common story is that as a young boy in New Orleans, he scooped coins from the street and stuck them in his mouth to prevent theft, earning the nickname "satchel mouth"; another is that his large mouth led to the nickname. Early on, he was known as "Dipper," short for "Dippermouth," referencing the song *Dippermouth Blues*. The nickname "Pops" came from Armstrong's habit of forgetting names and calling people "Pops," which was later used as a title for a 2010 biography by Terry Teachout. After a Savoy competition, he was crowned "King Menelik," after the Emperor of Ethiopia, for slaying "ofay jazz demons." Armstrong celebrated his identity as a Black man from a poor New Orleans neighborhood and avoided "putting on airs," though many younger Black musicians criticized him for performing in segregated audiences and not taking a stronger stand.

Louis Armstrong was known by several nicknames, including "satchel mouth," which originated from his large mouth, a trait that led to the nickname being shortened to "Satchmo," and "Dipper," short for "Dippermouth," referencing the song "Dippermouth Blues" and his unique embouchure. He was also called "Pops" because he often forgot people's names and referred to them as such, a nickname later used as the title of a 2010 biography by Terry Teachout. After a competition at the Savoy, he was dubbed "King Menelik" after the Emperor of Ethiopia for defeating "ofay jazz demons." Armstrong celebrated his identity as a Black man from a poor New Orleans neighborhood and avoided appearing elitist; however, younger Black musicians criticized him for performing in segregated audiences and not actively supporting the civil rights movement. In 1957, during a candid interview in Grand Forks, North Dakota, shortly after the Little Rock desegregation crisis, Armstrong denounced Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus and President Dwight D. Eisenhower, calling the President "two-faced" and "having no guts," and stated he would cancel a planned Soviet Union tour, saying, "The way they're treating my people in the South, the government can go to hell." The FBI maintained a file on him due to his outspoken views on integration. His comments drew both praise and backlash, with figures like Jackie Robinson and Lena Horne supporting him, while a Mississippi radio station banned his records; his longtime manager, Pierre Tallerie, attempted to retract the remarks, prompting Armstrong to sharply rebuke him and insist on speaking for himself. When asked about his religion, Armstrong said he was raised Baptist, wore a Star of David in honor of the Karnoffsky family who supported him as a child and lent him money to buy his first cornet, was baptized Catholic at the Sacred Heart of Jesus Church in New Orleans, and met Pope Pius XII and Pope Paul VI. Armstrong was concerned about his health and used laxatives to manage his weight, a practice he promoted in his diet plan "Lose Weight the Satchmo Way"; he initially used Pluto Water but became a strong advocate for Swiss Kriss, even distributing packets to people including members of the British royal family. He also created humorous risqué cards featuring himself sitting on a toilet viewed through a keyhole with the slogan "Satch says, 'Leave it all behind ya!'"—a claim sometimes mistakenly described as advertising Swiss Kriss. In a live recording of "Baby, It's Cold Outside" with Velma Middleton, he altered the lyric to "Take some Swiss Kriss while I pour." His laxative use began in childhood when his mother collected dandelions and peppergrass for her children's health. Armstrong was a heavy marijuana smoker throughout much of his life and was arrested in 1930 for drug possession, spending nine days in jail; he described marijuana as "a thousand times better than whiskey." His love of food is reflected in songs like "Cheesecake," "Cornet Chop Suey," and "Struttin' with Some Barbecue," though the latter was about a companion, not food, and he often signed his letters "Red beans and ricely yours." A fan of Major League Baseball, he founded a team in New Orleans called the Raggedy Nine and later transformed it into his "Secret Nine Baseball." Armstrong was gregarious and wrote constantly on the road, recording music, sex, food, childhood memories, his marijuana use, and even his bowel movements. He was not a Freemason; although sometimes cited as a member of Montgomery Lodge No. 18 (Prince Hall) in New York, no such lodge existed, and in his autobiography he stated he was a member of the Knights of Pythias of North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australia, an African American fraternal organization. In 1949, he presided as King of the Zulu Social Aid & Pleasure Club during Mardi Gras, earning a cover feature in Time magazine. Early in his career, Armstrong was renowned for his cornet and trumpet virtuosity, known for "clarinet-like figurations and high notes" and his "intense rhythmic 'swing'" involving accented upbeats, slurring, and complementary rhythmic patterns. His most celebrated recordings include the Hot Five and Hot Seven sessions and those with the Red Onion Jazz Babies; his improvisations, though unconventional, were subtle and melodic, with the solo in "Potato Head Blues" widely regarded as his best. Prior to Armstrong, jazz ensembles typically varied melodies; he was virtually the first to base significant variations on chord harmonies rather than melodies, transforming jazz into a soloist's art form. He often re-composed pop tunes with more compelling variations and composed over 50 original songs, including jazz standards like "Gully Low Blues," "Potato Head Blues," and "Swing That Music." He performed with major artists such as Bing Crosby, Duke Ellington, Fletcher Henderson, Earl Hines, Jimmie Rodgers, Bessie Smith, and Ella Fitzgerald; Crosby notably emulated Armstrong's vocal techniques, including easing breath, using head voice, and singing on consonants, which influenced later popular singers. Armstrong recorded two albums with Ella Fitzgerald—Ella and Louis and Ella and Louis Again—with backing by the Oscar Peterson Trio and drummer Buddy Rich on the first and Louie Bellson on the second; Norman Granz later envisioned a Porgy and Bess recording. His Columbia Records albums, Louis Armstrong Plays W.C. Handy (1954) and Satch Plays Fats (all Fats Waller tunes) (1955), were both masterpieces and moderately successful. In 1961, the All-Stars recorded The Great Summit and The Great Reunion (combined) with Duke Ellington, featuring many of Ellington's famous compositions and two exclusive tracks, with Ellington playing piano. His performance in Dave Brubeck's The Real Ambassadors (1963) was critically acclaimed and included "Summer Song," one of his most popular vocals. In the week beginning May 9, 1964, his recording of "Hello, Dolly!" reached number one, and the album of the same name also hit number one, displacing The Beatles and selling well, eventually going "Gold" (500,000); it won best male pop vocal performance at the 1964 Grammy Awards. Armstrong had 19 "Top Ten" records, including "Stardust," "What a Wonderful World," "When The Saints Go Marching In," "Dream a Little Dream of Me," "Ain't Misbehavin'," "You Rascal You," and "Stompin' at the Savoy"; "We Have All the Time in the World" gained renewed popularity in the UK in 1994 via a Guinness ad, reaching number 3. In 1964, Armstrong became the oldest artist to have a number one song with "Hello, Dolly!" and his song "Bout Time" was later featured in the film Bewitched. In February 1968, he performed "Grassa e Bella" in Italian on the Italian RAI television channel with Lara Saint Paul for the C.D.I. label. In 1968, "What a Wonderful World" topped the British charts for a month. He appeared on Johnny Cash's show on October 28, 1970, singing "Ramblin' Rose" and re-creating Jimmie Rodgers' "Blue Yodel No. 9" with Cash. Armstrong enjoyed diverse music, from blues to Guy Lombardo's arrangements, Latin American folk songs, and classical symphonies and opera, often incorporating these influences, which sometimes surprised fans. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as an early influence, with solos like the hard-rocking version of "St. Louis Blues" from the WC Handy album showing mutual influence. He appeared in over a dozen Hollywood films, most notably as a bandleader and narrator in the 1956 musical High Society, starring Bing Crosby, Grace Kelly, Frank Sinatra, and Celeste Holm, where he sang the title song and performed "Now You Has Jazz" with Crosby. In 1947, he played himself in New Orleans, opposite Billie Holiday, chronicling the decline of Storyville and the exodus of musicians from New Orleans to Chicago; in The Five Pennies (1959), he played himself, sang, and performed classic numbers, including a duet with Danny Kaye, during which Kaye impersonated Armstrong. He also appeared in The Glenn Miller Story alongside James Stewart. In 1937, Armstrong became the first African American to host a nationally broadcast radio show. In 1969, he had a cameo in Gene Kelly's Hello, Dolly! as the bandleader Louis, singing the title song with Barbra Streisand. He appeared on radio programs such as The Story of Swing (1937) and This Is Jazz (1947), and made television appearances, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, including on The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. In 1949, his life was dramatized by Richard Durham in the Chicago WMAQ radio series Destination Freedom. Argentine writer Julio Cortázar, a self-described admirer, claimed that a 1952 concert at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris inspired his creation of the fictional creatures Cronopios, calling Armstrong "Grandísimo Cronopio." A pivotal scene in Stardust Memories (1980) features Woody Allen being overwhelmed by a recording of Armstrong's "Stardust" and experiencing a nostalgic epiphany. In 2022, a documentary film titled Louis Armstrong's Black & Blues was released about him. Against his doctor's advice, Armstrong played a two-week engagement at the Waldorf-Astoria's Empire Room in March 1971, after which he suffered a heart attack and was hospitalized; he was released in May and resumed trumpet practice. Still hoping to return to performing, he died of a heart attack in his sleep on July 6, 1971, in Corona, Queens, New York City. He was buried in Flushing Cemetery, Flushing, Queens, New York City. His honorary pallbearers included Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Pearl Bailey, Count Basie, Harry James, Frank Sinatra, Ed Sullivan, Earl Wilson, Benny Goodman, Alan King, Johnny Carson, and David Frost. Peggy Lee sang "The Lord's Prayer," Al Hibbler sang "Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen," and Fred Robbins, a longtime friend, delivered the eulogy. Armstrong was posthumously awarded the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972 by the Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, recognizing outstanding artistic contributions to the recording field. Recordings of Armstrong were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, established in 1973, to honor recordings at least 25 years old with qualitative or historical significance.

Louis Armstrong died, and was interred in Flushing Cemetery, Flushing, in Queens, New York City. His honorary pallbearers included Bing Crosby, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Pearl Bailey, Count Basie, Harry James, Frank Sinatra, Ed Sullivan, Earl Wilson, Benny Goodman, Alan King, Johnny Carson, and David Frost. Peggy Lee performed "The Lord's Prayer" at the services, Al Hibbler sang "Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen," and Fred Robbins, a long-time friend, delivered the eulogy. Armstrong was posthumously awarded the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972 by the Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, a Special Merit Award given by vote of the Recording Academy's National Trustees to performers who have made outstanding artistic contributions to the recording field. Recordings of Armstrong were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, established in 1973, to honor recordings that are at least 25 years old and have qualitative or historical significance. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame included Armstrong's "West End Blues" on its list of 500 songs that shaped rock and roll. In 1995, the U.S. Post Office issued a Louis Armstrong 32-cent commemorative postage stamp. In 1999, Armstrong was nominated for inclusion in the American Film Institute's 100 Years ... 100 Stars. In 1950, Bing Crosby, the most successful vocalist of the first half of the 20th century, stated, "He is the beginning and the end of music in America." Duke Ellington, in a 1971 DownBeat magazine article, said, "If anybody was a master, it was Louis Armstrong. He was and will continue to be the embodiment of jazz." Though Armstrong is widely recognized as a pioneer of scat singing, Ethel Waters and others had recorded scat singing in the 1920s prior to him, according to Gary Giddins and others. Literary critic Harold Bloom stated, "The two great American contributions to the world's art, in the end, are Walt Whitman and, after him, Armstrong and jazz ... If I had to choose between the two, ultimately, I wouldn't. I would say that the genius of this nation at its best is indeed Walt Whitman and Louis Armstrong." In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Armstrong at No. 39 on their list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time. In 1991, an asteroid was named 9179 Satchmo in his honor. In the summer of 2001, to commemorate the centennial of his birth, New Orleans's main airport was renamed Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport; the entrance to the airport's former terminal building features a statue depicting Armstrong playing his cornet. In 2002, Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–1928) were preserved in the United States National Recording Registry, selected annually by the National Recording Preservation Board for inclusion in the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry. The US Open tennis tournament's former main stadium was named Louis Armstrong Stadium in his honor, as Armstrong had lived a few blocks from the site. Congo Square, a historic gathering place for Black people in New Orleans for dancing and music, was later renamed Louis Armstrong Park. Dedicated in April 1980, the park includes a 12-foot (3.7 m) statue of Armstrong holding a trumpet. A Wonderful World, a musical based on his life, had its world premiere run at Miami New Drama from December 4, 2021, to January 16, 2021, after mounting previews beginning March 5, 2020, and canceling opening night (March 14) due to COVID concerns. Mirroring Armstrong's musical journey, the show stars James Monroe Iglehart and makes "pre-Broadway" stops in New Orleans on October 1–8, 2023, and Chicago on October 11–29, 2023. The musical, conceived by Drama Desk Award winner and Tony Award nominee Christopher Renshaw and novelist Andrew Delaplaine, and directed by Renshaw, features an original book by Aurin Squire and charts the rise of Armstrong from the perspective of his four wives. The show will debut on Broadway in 2024. The house where Armstrong lived for nearly 28 years was declared a National Historic Landmark and opened to the public for guided tours in 2003. The Louis Armstrong House Museum, located at 34–56 107th Street between 34th and 37th avenues in Corona, Queens, presents concerts and educational programs, operates as a historic house museum, and makes its archives of writings, books, recordings, and memorabilia available for public research. The museum is administered by Queens College, City University of New York, following the terms of Lucille Armstrong's will, and is operated by the nonprofit Louis Armstrong House Museum. It opened to the public on October 15, 2003. A new visitors center opened across the street from the Armstrong home in the summer of 2023. The museum's website includes the digitized Armstrong Archives, searchable 24 hours a day.
